food.text: Pemmican, a mixture of tallow and dried meat, was the concentrated food of choice for polar travel. The American explorer Robert Peary carried it on all three of his Arctic expeditions between 1886 and 1909, feeding it to both his men and his dogs.

Pemmican - a calorie-rich mixture of tallow and dried meat - became the staple food of polar exploration. Arctic and Antarctic explorers such as Fridtjof Nansen, Robert Falcon Scott, Ernest Shackleton, Roald Amundsen and Robert Peary all carried it to sustain their expeditions.

Whalers hunted whales in the Arctic and North Atlantic for their meat and blubber, valued as food, and for oil rendered from the blubber that became important to the Industrial Revolution. Demand for this whale oil, sometimes called 'train oil', surged during the 19th century and spurred the development of new whaling techniques.

Traditional Inuit food was eaten mostly frozen, raw, or boiled, with very little mixture of ingredients and few added spices. Because the Arctic climate was ill-suited to agriculture, this diet of fished, hunted and gathered animal foods was higher in fat and protein than the global average.

Robert Peary called pemmican an absolute necessity for polar travel. He wrote that 'without it a sledge-party cannot compact its supplies within a limit of weight to make a serious polar journey successful.'
Inuit hunters often ate their catch frozen, consuming it right where the animal was killed. This custom was believed to keep the blood flowing and the body warm in the Arctic cold.

According to a custom recorded by Heinrich Klutschak, fish could not be eaten cooked at the spot where it was caught, only raw. Cooking was permitted, over a blubber lamp, only once hunters had travelled a full day's march from the fishing site.

art.text: In 1823–1824 the German Romantic painter Caspar David Friedrich painted The Sea of Ice, his interpretation of an Arctic landscape with a shipwreck half-buried in the ice. Its radical composition and subject were unusual for the time, and the work was met with incomprehension. It is now considered one of his masterpieces.
The history of Greenlandic painting began with Aron von Kangeq in the mid-19th century. In his drawings and watercolours he depicted the old Greenlandic sagas and myths.

In 1905 an angakkuq, or spirit healer, named Mitsivarniannga from Ammassalik Island made a tupilaq, an "evil spirit object", for a visiting European. When no harm befell him for making and showing it to an outsider, others began making tupilait. The objects evolved into a popular art form.
Johann Gottlob von Quandt commissioned The Sea of Ice from Friedrich. He wanted two paintings, one of southern nature and one of northern nature.
The critic Russell Potter has hailed The Sea of Ice as a key instance of the "Arctic Sublime". He also sees it as an influence on later nineteenth-century polar paintings.

Friedrich probably became familiar with William Edward Parry's expedition to find the Northwest Passage through published accounts of North Pole expeditions. In the winter of 1820–21 he made extensive oil studies of ice floes on the river Elbe, near Dresden. These were probably incorporated into The Sea of Ice.

The Sea of Ice was first exhibited at the Prague Academy exhibition of 1824. It was titled An Idealized Scene of an Arctic Sea, with a Wrecked Ship on the Heaped Masses of Ice. Before 1826 it was called The Polar Sea.
The Sea of Ice was still unsold when Friedrich died in 1840. It is now held by the Kunsthalle Hamburg in Hamburg.

Commentators have linked The Sea of Ice to Théodore Géricault's 'The Raft of the Medusa'. Some scholars also speculate that Friedrich's childhood trauma influenced it: on 8 December 1787 his brother Johann Christoffer fell through the ice on a body of water and died. It has been rumored that Friedrich might have forced his brother onto the ice. Friedrich's influences for the painting are unconfirmed.

war.text: The Lady Franklin Bay Expedition of 1881 to 1884 was promoted by the United States Army Signal Corps and led by Lieutenant Adolphus Greely of the Fifth United States Cavalry. Of the original twenty-five officers and men who traveled to Ellesmere Island, only six survived to return.

Fort Conger was built in 1881 on Ellesmere Island as a military and scientific outpost for the Lady Franklin Bay Expedition, led by Lieutenant Adolphus Greely. Greely named it after U.S. Senator Omar D. Conger, who had backed the expedition, and twenty-five officers, enlisted men, and Inuit lived and worked there.

The British Arctic Expedition of 1875 to 1876 was sent by the British Admiralty under Sir George Nares to try to reach the North Pole via Smith Sound. Two Royal Navy ships, HMS Alert and HMS Discovery, sailed from Portsmouth in May 1875 but found only ice instead of the hoped-for open polar sea.

From 1839 to 1843, Royal Navy captain James Clark Ross led an expedition to Antarctica using two unusually strong warships, HMS Erebus and HMS Terror. The voyage confirmed the existence of the Antarctic continent and discovered the Ross Ice Shelf, Mount Erebus, and Mount Terror.

As starvation spread during the Lady Franklin Bay Expedition, Lieutenant Adolphus Greely ordered the execution of Private Henry for repeatedly stealing food from the party's dwindling supplies. Most of the other men died of starvation, hypothermia, or drowning before a rescue party finally reached them in 1884.

In June 1884, a rescue squadron commanded by Commander Winfield Scott Schley, including USS Bear, USS Thetis, HMS Alert, and Loch Garry, reached the Lady Franklin Bay Expedition's camp on June 22. Only seven of the original twenty-five men had survived the winter; the rest had died of starvation, hypothermia, and drowning, and Private Henry had been executed on Greely's order for repeated theft of food. One of the seven rescued, Joseph Elison, died on July 8 after multiple amputations.

During the British Arctic Expedition, a sledging party under Commander Albert Hastings Markham set a new Farthest North record of 83° 20′ 26″ N. The article calls the expedition overall a near-disaster: the men suffered badly from scurvy and were hampered by inappropriate clothing and equipment. Nares realised his men could not survive another winter in the ice and hastily retreated south with both ships in the summer of 1876.

Before Fort Conger existed, the crew of HMS Discovery under Sir George Nares wintered at the same Discovery Harbour site during the British Arctic Expedition of 1875. Nares left behind provisions there, but most of these supplies could no longer be found when Greely's men built Fort Conger in 1881.

In 1845, Rear-Admiral Sir John Franklin led HMS Erebus and HMS Terror to find the Northwest Passage, with Francis Crozier commanding Terror. The ships became icebound off King William Island, and Franklin died there in June 1847. The ships were abandoned ten months later, and the entire crew died of starvation, hypothermia and scurvy. Inuit accounts told of men who had succumbed to the cold and some who resorted to cannibalism, and in 1997 cut marks from blades were found on crew bones on King William Island, with evidence of bones broken and boiled to extract marrow.

literature.text: Before Greenlandic had a written tradition, Inuit culture there kept a rich body of legends and myths alive through oral tradition. In the 19th century these narratives were collected, most notably by Hinrich Johannes Rink in western Greenland.

The only first-hand information on the progress of Franklin's lost expedition is a two-part written message called the Victory Point Note, found on King William Island. It is the last known communication from the expedition.

In his 1903 book The Arctic Home in the Vedas, the Indian nationalist Bal Gangadhar Tilak analysed Vedic hymns and Avestan passages. He argued that the North Pole was the original home of the Aryans, and that the last ice age destroyed that home and its warm climate. Only the surviving Aryans left, around 8000 B.C., searching for new lands in the northern parts of Europe and Asia.
literature.source_title: The Arctic Home in the Vedas
tags: The Arctic Home in the Vedas

literature.text: In the 19th century, Greenlandic literature was strongly influenced by Christian hymnody. Figures such as Rasmus Berthelsen, Henrik Lund and Jonathan Petersen played a central role in this development.

In 1859, Francis Leopold McClintock published The Voyage of the Fox in the Arctic Seas, an account of his 1857 to 1859 voyage aboard the Fox in search of Franklin. He found the remains of two crewmen from Erebus on King William Island, together with the ship's boat and other detritus. The expedition's 129 men had vanished into the ice after 1845. In 1854 John Rae had already found dead bodies on King William Island and reported suspicions of cannibalism among the last survivors.
tags: The Voyage of the Fox in the Arctic Seas

literature.text: In classical and medieval literature, ultima Thule came to mean any distant place beyond the borders of the known world. By the 19th century, writers frequently identified Thule with Norway, Denmark, all of Scandinavia, a large Scottish island or the Faroes.

The second part of the Victory Point Note is dated 25 April 1848 and signed by Fitzjames and Crozier. It records that Franklin had died on 11 June 1847, and that the total loss by deaths in the expedition was 9 officers and 15 men. The 105 survivors, by then having abandoned the ships, planned to start walking the next day toward the Back River on the Canadian mainland. From archaeological finds it is believed that all of them died on that march of about 400 km, most on the island.
The Latin phrase for "farthest Thule" also became the title of a poetry collection. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow published Ultima Thule in 1880.

Greenland's Inuit legends and myths were preserved through oral tradition before writing arrived. In the 19th century they were collected, most notably by Hinrich Johannes Rink in western Greenland. Greenlandic literature of that century was also strongly influenced by Christian hymnody, with figures such as Rasmus Berthelsen, Henrik Lund, and Jonathan Petersen playing a central role.

Tilak wrote The Arctic Home in the Vedas at the end of 1898, but it was first published in Pune only in March 1903. He cited William F. Warren's Paradise Found or the Cradle of the Human Race at the North Pole as having anticipated his ideas.
literature.source_title: The Arctic Home in the Vedas
tags: The Arctic Home in the Vedas

science.text: Yakov Sannikov and Matvei Gedenschtrom claimed to have seen a land mass during their 1809–1810 cartographic expedition to the New Siberian Islands. Sannikov was the first to report a "new land" north of Kotelny Island in 1811, which gave Sannikov Land its name. It became something of a myth in 19th-century Russia.

Andrée's Arctic balloon expedition of 1897 was a failed Swedish effort to reach the North Pole. S. A. Andrée proposed a hydrogen balloon voyage from Svalbard to Russia or Canada, passing over the North Pole on the way. The balloon crashed on the pack ice after two days, and Andrée, Knut Frænkel and Nils Strindberg, inadequately clothed, equipped and prepared, made a grueling trek south until they ended up exhausted on Kvitøya and died there in October. Strindberg, the youngest, died first and was "buried" by the others, wedged into a cliff aperture. What killed them is still contested: trichinosis from undercooked polar bear meat, a polar bear attack, and cold and exhaustion have all been proposed.

In England and other European nations, a persistent myth held that an "Open Polar Sea" lay beyond the Arctic ice. John Barrow, longtime Second Secretary of the British Admiralty, promoted exploration of the region from 1818 to 1845 in search of it. Explorers who travelled closer to the pole reported thick, year-round ice, and the theory was widely considered disproven by the early 1900s.

In August 1901, during the Russian Polar Expedition led by Baron Eduard von Toll, the ship Zarya crossed the Laptev Sea searching for Sannikov Land. It was blocked by pack ice, and in 1902 the Zarya was trapped in fast ice. In November, Toll and three companions left the ship and travelled south on loose ice floes, away from Bennett Island, and vanished forever.

Nils Strindberg, a brilliant student doing original research in physics and chemistry, was chosen for Andrée's expedition. The main scientific purpose was to map the area by aerial photography. Strindberg was a devoted amateur photographer and a skilled constructor of advanced cameras.

In the 1850s and 1860s, American explorers Elisha Kane and Isaac Israel Hayes both claimed to have seen part of the Open Polar Sea. Even late in the century, the eminent authority Matthew Fontaine Maury described it in his textbook The Physical Geography of the Sea (1883).
tags: The Physical Geography of the Sea

science.text: During the Polaris expedition of the early 1870s, American Charles Francis Hall became the first outsider to see northwest Greenland. This came decades before Denmark's first permanent settlement in the northwest in 1909. From 1886 to 1909, American Robert Peary was the first outsider to explore far northern Greenland.
science.source_title: Proposed United States acquisition of Greenland

science.text: Some historians and geographers think Sannikov Land once existed but was destroyed by coastal erosion and became a submerged sand shoal, like other islands made of fossilized ice or permafrost. Others suggest it was a mirage of Bennett Island, and such mirages occur frequently in the Arctic.

Andrée ignored early warning signs about his plan. The polar balloon Örnen (Eagle) was delivered to Svalbard from its Paris manufacturer without being tested. When measurements showed it leaking more gas than expected, Andrée failed to acknowledge the risk, and there was much evidence that his drag-rope steering technique was ineffective.

In 1867, Secretary of State William H. Seward requested a United States Coast Survey report on Greenland and Iceland. Published in 1868, it very positively described Greenland's "unusual healthfulness" and large amounts of fish, game, and minerals. Seward wanted it to encourage Americans to support a possible purchase.
science.source_title: Proposed United States acquisition of Greenland

science.text: Andrée picked Nils Gustaf Ekholm, an experienced Arctic meteorological researcher, for his 1896 launch attempt. Ekholm had been Andrée's boss during an 1882–1883 geophysical expedition to Spitsbergen.

Andrée was reverentially called Ingenjör Andrée, a title expressing esteem for the late 19th-century ideal of the engineer as a representative of social improvement through technological progress. At a 1895 lecture for the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, he thrilled an audience of geographers and meteorologists.

politics.text: The United States has talked about obtaining Greenland from Denmark since the 19th century. Secretary of State William H. Seward advocated buying it in 1867, and the idea came up in the federal government again in 1910.
politics.source_title: Proposed United States acquisition of Greenland

politics.text: On March 30, 1867, the United States purchased Alaska from the Russian Empire. That purchase made it one of the eight Arctic nations and one of the five Arctic Ocean littoral countries.
politics.source_title: Arctic policy of the United States

politics.text: When Denmark and Norway separated in 1814, Greenland was transferred from the Norwegian to the Danish crown. The Treaty of Kiel severed Norway's former colonies and left them under the control of the Danish monarch.

In 1867 Seward considered annexing both Greenland and Iceland an idea "worthy of serious consideration". A government-published report described Greenland's "unusual healthfulness" and its fish, game and minerals, and predicted annexation would encourage Canada to join the United States.
politics.source_title: Proposed United States acquisition of Greenland

politics.text: Britain claimed the far north of Canada as part of the British Arctic Territories, and in 1880 it transferred that claim to Canada. Canada incorporated the far north into the Northwest Territories. The Inuit were unaware, for some time, that their lands had just been included in Canada under international law.

The Canadian government purchased the Hudson's Bay Company's claim to Rupert's Land in 1869. Canada then renamed the purchased area the Northwest Territories and made a series of treaties with local First Nations over land title.

Pressed by Franklin's wife, Jane, and others, the Admiralty launched a search for the missing Franklin expedition in 1848. In 1854 John Rae was told by an Inuk that 35 to 40 white men had died of starvation near the mouth of the Back River, and other Inuit confirmed the story, including reports of cannibalism among the dying sailors. Later searches found skeletons, including two in a lifeboat on King William Island, and bones bearing cut marks that support the cannibalism allegations.
Gold was discovered in the Yukon in 1896, leading to the Klondike Gold Rush of 1896-1899. To deal with the increased settlement, the Canadian government created the Yukon Territory in 1898.

During the Polaris expedition of the early 1870s, American Charles Francis Hall was the first outsider to see northwest Greenland. From 1886 to 1909, Robert Peary explored far northern Greenland and unofficially claimed much of it for the United States, before Denmark's first permanent settlement in the northwest in 1909.
politics.source_title: Proposed United States acquisition of Greenland

politics.text: Owners of the British bark Chance first made a claim against the United States for whaling losses on 15 February 1872. After the Earl of Derby intervened in 1877, the matter went to Congress, and the President signed a relief bill in April 1890, almost nineteen years after the event.

In 1886 the US Senate raised the relief for the British bark Chance from $10,000 to $15,500 to cover fifteen years' interest. This broke with the tradition of not allowing interest, because the funds were owed to foreign people.

philosophy.text: The name Thule, first written of by the Greek explorer Pytheas, came to mean any distant place beyond the borders of the known world. By the 19th century it was frequently identified with Norway, Denmark, the whole of Scandinavia, one of the larger Scottish islands, or the Faroes. Earlier, Ultima Thule had sometimes been a Latin name for Greenland, when Thule itself was used for Iceland.

Danish geologist and Greenlandic scholar Hinrich Johannes Rink wrote in the 19th century about the Amarok, a gigantic wolf in Inuit religion. He reported that Greenlandic Inuit reserve the word exclusively for this legendary wolf, while other Arctic peoples use it for any wolf. The Amarok was said to stalk and devour any person foolish enough to hunt alone at night, unlike ordinary wolves, which hunt in packs.

Historical documentation of Inuit spiritual traditions comes largely from Christian missionaries and explorers, as well as anthropologists active since the late 19th century. Missionaries in Canada were often interested in recording Inuit traditions, even as they worked to spread Christianity.

Nineteenth-century antiquarians and historians argued over where Thule really lay. The British surveyor Charles Vallancey argued that Ireland was Thule. In 1876 the Scottish historian W.F. Skene identified it as the Kintyre peninsula, based on a description given by Solinus.

The idea of Thule kept its poetic pull into the late 19th century. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow published a collection called Ultima Thule in 1880. In 1910 the explorer Knud Rasmussen gave the name Thule to a missionary and trading post he established at North Star Bay in northwest Greenland.

culture.text: In the 19th century, Inuit of continental North America suffered substantial population decline, largely because of newly introduced diseases. Increasingly, Inuit were employed by whalers, an economic change that contributed to cultural change. Ethnographic accounts from the period record the decline of many customs, such as the tattooing of women.

In Canada, the first Anglican mission post among Inuit was established in 1894, and the first Roman Catholic post was created at Chesterfield Inlet (Igluligaarjuk) in 1912. Christianity subsequently spread rapidly among Canada's Inuit population.

In the 19th century, Inuit of continental North America suffered substantial population decline, largely due to the introduction of new diseases. Europeans generally perceived the demise of Inuit culture to be inevitable, and white ethnographers such as Franz Boas and Knud Rasmussen hoped to document Inuit culture before it disappeared.

The Sadlermiut lived in near isolation on and around Coats Island, Walrus Island and Southampton Island in Hudson Bay until 1902–03. Scholars had thought they might be the last remnants of the Dorset culture, since their culture and dialect differed from the mainland Inuit. Encounters with Europeans and exposure to infectious disease caused the deaths of the last members of the Sadlermiut.
The orthography of Greenlandic, the language of most Greenlanders, was established in 1851. It was later revised in 1973.

When John Ross led an expedition into their territory in 1818, the Inughuit of northern Greenland were first contacted by Europeans. They are believed to have lived in total isolation before then. They are cited as one of the rare non-agricultural societies to live without armed feuds or warfare, a state that continued after contact.
